title: T1568 — Dynamic Resolution
subtitle: The animation below shows one full attack day in a small company network.

nodes.label: Sensitive data
nodes.tip: Sensitive data - What is at risk

steps.title: Register a throwaway domain
steps.caption: The attacker registers a cheap, short-lived domain and points its name server records at a server they control. The plan is simple: the name may live only a few days, so defenders have little time to react, and the registration itself leaves the first clue in registrar and passive DNS data
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: DGA makes candidate names
steps.caption: Malware on the victim laptop runs a domain generation algorithm. It computes a list of fake-looking names for today and starts asking the company resolver about them. Most names do not exist yet, so the resolver answers NXDOMAIN again and again. The resolver log now shows one host with many random labels - a strong early signal
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Resolver forwards upstream
steps.caption: The company resolver has no answer for these names, so it does its job and asks the authoritative name server on the internet. That server belongs to the attacker. The resolver's outbound lookups and its log entries connect the victim to the attacker's infrastructure
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Fast-flux answer, TTL 30
steps.caption: One of the DGA names is actually registered today. The attacker's name server answers with an IP that changes at every query, and a TTL of 30 seconds keeps caches small. Within two minutes the same name has returned several different IPs, often in different networks. This IP churn is the fast-flux layer in action
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: DNS calculation channel
steps.caption: The malware hides data inside the query itself. It packs its host ID and the next request into a long label such as a1f3..9c.task.c2tld[.]com . The attacker's name server decodes the label and learns which machine is calling and what it needs. The company sees only ordinary-looking DNS questions, but their labels are far longer than any human name
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Beacon to the real C2
steps.caption: The name server answers with the real C2 IP inside the A record. The malware now beacons to the C2 server over HTTPS every 60 seconds. On the network this looks like small, regular, boring sessions - to a brand-new domain and IP that nobody has seen before
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: SOC correlation fires
steps.caption: The SOC dashboard links the pieces: a high NXDOMAIN ratio, very low TTLs, IP churn, and a beacon to a first-seen domain, all from one host. A correlation alert goes to the analyst with the host name and a risk score. This is the detection moment - four weak signals become one strong case
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Block, sinkhole, and hunt
steps.caption: The analyst blocks the domain at the resolver with a response policy and blocks the C2 IPs at the firewall. Then they use passive DNS to hunt backwards and find three more hosts that talked to the same infrastructure earlier. The attack channel is dead, and the wider campaign is now visible
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.
